subject: history
title: Civil Rights: Significance and Legacy
welcome_lead: Today you'll stretch — what did the rights movements really change, and what remained?
meta_desc: GCSE History stretch — significance and legacy of civil rights movements, interpretations and continuing struggles.
final_note: You can now judge significance, weigh interpretations and connect the past to today.

concepts.def: How important an event was, short or long term
Long-term impact left behind by events or people
Separation by custom rather than by law
Post-apartheid hearings to face past abuses
1970 UK law requiring equal pay for equal work

walkthroughs.body_html:
Strong answers ask: did this change laws, lives or attitudes — and for how long?

The Civil Rights Act (1964) was hugely significant in law. But de facto segregation in housing and schools continued. Significance isn't the same as total success.

Some historians stress Martin Luther King and peaceful protest.

Others highlight Malcolm X, the Black Panthers and the role of grassroots activists — many of them women like Ella Baker. Both views use evidence; the best answers combine them.

In Britain, the Equal Pay Act (1970) and Race Relations Acts shaped law. In South Africa, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after 1995 tried to heal divisions.

Modern movements like Black Lives Matter (founded 2013) show that the legacy continues — the work isn't over.

mcqs.q: What did Brown v Board of Education decide in 1954?
options: Rosa Parks was the lawyer who argued Brown v Board.
Brown v Board of Education immediately desegregated all schools in America.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
The Supreme Court ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v Ferguson and beginning legal dismantling of school segregation.

mcqs.q: How was the US civil rights movement achieved?
options: Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Through decades of mass organising — NAACP legal work, grassroots campaigns, sit-ins, freedom rides — alongside leaders like King and Malcolm X.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Martin Luther King's 'I Have a Dream' speech ended segregation.

mcqs.q: Was Rosa Parks's refusal to give up her bus seat a spontaneous act?
options: No — Parks was a trained NAACP activist; the boycott was organised by long-standing civil rights networks that turned her arrest into a planned campaign.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Rosa Parks was just a tired seamstress who refused on impulse to give up her seat.
Rosa Parks was the lawyer who argued Brown v Board.
